replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>Correct me if I am wrong but you made the claim that 80-90% margins mean the model is viable, would that not be on you to show?

I'm correcting you. You are wrong. The implicit claim being made is token costs are non-viable, by you. The onus is therefore on you to show that non-viability, which you haven't done.

There is no universal law that says API costs and subscription costs must have equal gross margins, nor are they identical goods. Nor are profits and costs equal even on a more fundamental level. Common belief, leaked data, [and Anthropic's own cited statements](https://www.reuters.com/business/retail-consumer/anthropic-tells-investors-it-will-be-profitable-second-straight-quarter-ft-2026-09-13/) (there's the 'show' you're asking for) point to 80%+ gross margins right now for what they're serving.

If you want to cast doubt those numbers, the onus is on you to disprove them or materially explain justifiable doubt. Right now you have little more than vague, empty doubt and pivots to non-equivalent net margins. Net is not gross.

replies.author: UncleRonnyJ
replies.body:
Thanks for the curtness, very kind of you.

Ok fair, 80%+ on serving tokens, no argument there. My problem is calling that viable. Reuters saw the draft S-1. 2025 was an $8B operating loss on $4.6B revenue. They’ve also signed up for $518B of compute over the next ten years, most of which they can’t get out of, and they had about $20B cash at the end of last year.

The Q2 profit in your link is adjusted and preliminary, and stock-based pay is left out of it. Revenue this year has been huge so maybe they turn it around, I genuinely don’t know. One adjusted quarter just doesn’t prove much to me when the filing looks like that.

Also your own numbers on the $13k guy. At 80-90% margin that’s still $1,300 to $2,600 of compute for someone paying $200.

Here’s the link: [https://www.reuters.com/business/anthropics-518-billion-ai-buildout-hinges-largely-deals-that-cannot-be-canceled-2026-09-29/](https://www.reuters.com/business/anthropics-518-billion-ai-buildout-hinges-largely-deals-that-cannot-be-canceled-2026-09-29/)

Same outlet as yours, a couple of weeks later and it’s from the draft S-1 rather than what Anthropic told investors.

replies.author: TitoZola
replies.body:
Honest question for both of you, not taking a side: isn't a token a meter rather than the thing being sold? What people pay for is intelligence, and tokens differ enormously in what they cost to serve and how much intelligence they carry.

If in two years a token costs the same but carries way more intelligence, was the margin on today's token ever the thing to argue about? And as the cost of today's level of intelligence keeps falling, does its price fall with it, or does the margin on it get absurdly insane?

replies.author: UncleRonnyJ
replies.body:
Good question. The price does fall. Epoch AI reckons the price for a fixed level of performance drops around 10x+ a year. But the top model stays expensive, and that's where the labs make their money. Most tokens on OpenRouter go to cheaper, older models anyway.
So the high margin only really holds on the newest models, and staying there means constant training, which is the bit the 80% leaves out.
https://epoch.ai/data-insights/llm-inference-price-trends

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>If in two years a token costs the same but carries way more intelligence, was the margin on today's token ever the thing to argue about? 

1. The token isn't the thing being sold, and neither, actually, is intelligence. What's being sold is an ecosystem centered around that intelligence. For instance, I pay OpenAI over Anthropic because OpenAI provides duplex voice and a full cloud agent and Anthropic doesn't. Anthropic's models are currently more intelligent, but OpenAI's ecosystem is (at least to me, but many others) more valuable.
2. You should assume the margins stay relatively constant, as competition forces the margins to stay constant. What also goes up is revenues as more capable ecosystems discover new uses and expand their total addressable market.
3. So no, the margins on today's tokens were never the thing to argue about, because not because of the margins, but because of the capability of the tokens themselves. A given gross margin on a small TAM is not comparable to a given gross margin on a large TAM in-aggregate — they imply totally different net margins.

This is also why the "but they're burning cash" arguments make no sense — of course they're burning cash. They're hyperscaling. Burning cash is the point and how you get to hyperscale, at which point the numbers look totally different. See Amazon circa 1999 and today, and what happened with AWS and marketplace.

cc u/UncleRonnyJ

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>They’ve also signed up for $518B of compute over the next ten years, most of which they can’t get out of, and they had about $20B cash at the end of last year.

They don't want to "get out of it". The LTAs specifically exist to lock in the prices. Suggesting they "can't get out of" the contracts is (and again, I'm going to be *ahem* curt here) pure dumbfuckery that misunderstands the entire situation.

When you're on a rocket ship to the moon, you're not looking to "get out of" that rocket ship. You're looking to lock in. 

Long-term agreements are risk amelioration for locking in.

replies.author: UncleRonnyJ
replies.body:
I never said they wanted out. I said most of it can't be cancelled, which is what the filing says. Locking in capacity is fine if demand keeps going up, I get that. But about 80% of it gets paid whether they use it or not, and a lot of the revenue to cover it isn't locked in. That's the risk. Your rocket ship only works if it keeps going up.
You also skipped the $8B operating loss and the Q2 profit leaving out stock-based pay.
And I'll assume the dumbfuckery wasn't aimed at me, seeing as I was just repeating what the filing says. Happy to leave it there, but only if you want 😛

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>Your rocket ship only works if it keeps going up.

Newsflash: The rocket not only keeps going up, it is accelerating.

We've done the equations, tested it, filled it with fuel, it's lifted off the pad, and is now in the stratosphere. Not only are the models getting more efficient, but the compute is getting more efficient, and those efficiencies are inherently recursive and compounding in nature.

The time for "will the rocket go up?" conversations was two years ago, when the rocket was fueled up and sitting on the pad. We've passed [Max Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_q) already. The rocket is going up.

replies.author: UncleRonnyJ
replies.body:
I'm not saying the rocket isn't going up. Revenue's huge, efficiency gains are real, no argument. My point is most of the $518B gets paid either way, so it's a bet on that growth keeping pace with the costs. And costs are climbing too. McKinsey found 93% of enterprises running AI agents are over their AI budgets.
Also Max Q is peak stress, not orbit. Rockets still fail after it.
I'll check back when the S-1s are public. Off to touch grass.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>I'm not saying the rocket isn't going up. 

You aren't. But you are also (and I'm going to torture the metaphor here, apologies, but stick with it) standing at the pad hemming at hawing that they spent so much on fuel and talking about how the fuel contracts are iron clad while agreeing the rocket is well-designed and now explicitly not denying the rocket is going up.

The rocket is going up. There are legitimate questions about the long-term solvency of any rocket program, but that isn't determined by program costs or fuel costs or profitability of a first launch with dummy payloads. 

>McKinsey found 93% of enterprises running AI agents are over their AI budgets.

I think you have to realize that we're still in the phase of companies "making it work before making it cheap", and that's true for both the inference providers and the inference consumers. Those McKinsey companies are full of 9-5ers slop-cannoning and token maxing their way towards KPIs mandated by their bosses as everyone scrambles to figure things out. 

It's all going to be inefficient as efficiencies are discovered. As efficiencies are discovered, budgets increase along with ROI — they are not a fixed ceiling. Since we agree the efficiencies (and general performance of the models) are going up, we implicitly agree this is all baked-in. The only questions left are who capitalizes on all of it.

I'm off to touch grass too (literally, there's fall gardening to get out of the way over here) but I hope that all makes sense.

replies.author: Recoil42
replies.body:
>My guess: once it gets this expensive

That's just the thing: It isn't getting expensive. Efficiency is going up — that's baked in. It's literally the reason why the industry is so confident and making such long bets.

For instance, I think a lot of people forget that for all intents and purposes, most 'AI' workloads are nearly all running on beefed up hand-me-down architectures from gaming graphics cards. We haven't even gotten to the point where bespoke neural architectures are doing the bulk of the gruntwork.

Spinning up a new fab takes three years and a datacenter takes two. The first neurally-optimized chips just hit this year, and the first neurally-designed chips won't hit until next year. GPT-3.5 is barely four years old, and the capex ramps just started to hit in 2024.

We haven't even *begun* to hit the bell curve of this tech. We're flatly way more early than you think.

replies.author: gravesisme
replies.body:
I'm a software engineer by trade and have been trying to level up my ways of working when it comes to AI tooling over the past couple months and purchased the $200 subscription to do that. I've been building an AI agent planning and orchestration tool, Planestro, that I plan to open source, which orchestrates a fleet of AI agents and handles things like worktree feature isolation, monitoring CI, isolating epic branches and merging them into develop when finished and making sure branches are properly rebased and merged with minimal human-in-the-loop - even if conflicts arise. I've been interested in figuring out how to surface the necessary human-in-the-loop elements, such as art review, music generation, and sound effects review and in the process I shipped a game, Hurricane Harrison, to the iOS App Store. I'm currently working on 5 new levels and improved graphics and gameplay for the steam release I'm planning. I find that "eating your own dogfood" works best for building out tooling and has helped me really sharpen the Planestro v1.0.0 release I have planned.

I wrote a blog post about it here if you are interested in technical detail:

[https://planestro.com/blog/building-an-ai-fleet/](https://planestro.com/blog/building-an-ai-fleet/)

replies.author: Many-Lie-6916
replies.body: You’re comparing apples and oranges. Uber is a transportation app, first popular as an extra job/income platform, now it’s basically a taxi app with most drivers working full time for a full living wage, in a world where fuel prices keep raising, and laws and taxes get tighter and stricter regarding vehicles all over the world, hence the price increase. Then there’s inflation too, of course. The point is that Uber is not scalable the same way as AI is, Uber is a product with an expiry date, but before then company will reinvent or move towards a replacement, like they’re testing with autonomous cars and flying taxis already. AI on other hand is a tool that scales in almost every direction and it needs one thing - compute power. It’s on a completely different scale in terms of what’s possible compared to Uber. Of course a lot of it is still subsidized today, but I think what they’re betting on is that as compute grows and models continue to improve and become more cost-effective, and the product gets adapted everywhere possible, the numbers will just even out. Only then comes the question of how much money they want or need(duty to investors) to make once they own a chunk of the market. When they say “AI race” they don’t mean only in terms of intelligence, it’s also a race of who will reach that profitability threshold first or gets ahead enough where they all the investor money pours to them and from there onwards it’s just a matter of scale.

replies.author: Ok-Past3775
replies.body:
Not at all.

Tokens will become more expensive for the heaviest features, but as the models develop they will able to do current tasks cheaper.

So tokens will get cheaper for "easier" tasks, while they will get more expensive for the heaviest tasks.

For example: Look at a scrawny kid. This kid, at year 1 struggles to pick up a 5kg weight. As the kid develops into a bodybuilder he will struggle lifting, let's say, 200kg, but it has become almost "inexpensive" energy and time wise for him to pick up the initial 5kg weight.

It will still take a lot for him to use the most of his capabilities, but he will be able to do everything that the older versions of him were doing, much cheaper and quicker.

comments.author: Realistic-Cookie5328
comments.body:
As models advance so will the need for more specialized hardware. 

And as models get larger to be trained at FP32, providers and companies to serve it at FP4 also will need to accommodate more buying or renting of hardware. 

Both of these will drive costs upward for the consumer who does not have the options of KV caching, pre-fix caching etc. available to make cost per token cheaper.
